newsitem.title: JAPAN: Richardson delays return from North Korea by a day.
newsitem.headline: Richardson delays return from North Korea by a day.

text.p: U.S. Congressman Bill Richardson postponed his planned departure from North Korea on Tuesday by one day but there was no sign the delay indicated a hitch in his plan to return home with American detainee Carl Hunziker.
A U.S. embassy spokesman in Tokyo told Reuters that the embassy was unaware so far of the reason for the delay in Richardson's plan to fly to Tokyo from Pyongyang.
"Mr Richardson will now arrive in Tokyo on Wednesday. There are still hopes that Mr Hunziker will be on the plane with the congressman when he leaves Pyongyang," the spokesman said.
Richardson flew from Tokyo to the North Korean capital on Monday in hopes of bringing back Hunziker, who was arrested on August 24 after crossing the Yalu River from China into North Korea.
Pyongyang has said it "proved by investigation" that Hunziker, 26, was a U.S. spy.
Hunziker's family has denied the charge, saying he is a missionary. U.S. and South Korean officials have denied that Hunziker was spying for their countries.
Analysts in Tokyo have said Pyongyang's plan to release Hunziker may help ease tensions between the North and South.
In another sign of a possible thawing in icy relations on the divided peninsula, Seoul on Tuesday sent home a rescued North Korean sailor.

Military officials said the sailor, Chung Kwang-son, private first class in North Korea's navy, was escorted by United Nations Command representatives and handed over to North Korean officers at the border village of Panmunjom.

The return of Chung was the first goodwill gesture by Seoul towards Pyongyang since already tense relations between the two Koreas worsened after a Pyongyang submarine landed 26 agents on a South Korean beach in September.
All but two of the 26 have been killed. One has been captured alive and another is still at large.
The North insists the grounding of the submarine was an accident and has demanded that Seoul return the bodies of the 24 agents.
Richardson, a Democrat from New Mexico close to the Clinton administration, had planned to visit North Korea in September but called off the trip after the submarine incident.
U.S. and North Korean officials have held meetings on the Hunziker case at the United Nations in New York.
Japan's Kyodo news agency has reported that Richardson aimed to get Hunziker's release in exchange for money. Hunziker's family have agreed to pay $5,000 for his release, the agency said.
Kyodo said North Korea had demanded $100,000 for Hunziker's release, but that the United States had rejected the demand on the grounds the amount was too high.

U.S. embassy officials in Tokyo had no comment on the Kyodo report. Richardson has served as a U.S. troubleshooter on several missions to countries that have no formal diplomatic ties with the United States, such as North Korea.
In December 1994, Richardson visited North Korea to negotiate the release of a U.S. pilot whose helicopter was brought down in North Korean airspace.
The two Koreas technically remain at war since the 1950-53 Korean War ended without a peace agreement.
